strengths: Addresses a practically important EDA problem (fast RTL quality estimation without invoking synthesis) with a well-motivated argument that CDFGs expose structural semantics more explicitly than token sequences used by prior LLM-based methods.

The two pretraining objectives (structure-aware masked node modeling on post-GNN embeddings, and edge prediction) are a thoughtful adaptation of graph SSL to CDFGs, explicitly designed to avoid the semantic ambiguity that arises from masking raw operator nodes/edges in computational graphs -- a reasonable and somewhat novel technical insight.

Combines structural pretraining with a cross-stage knowledge distillation strategy from post-mapping netlists, and shows this benefits both the proposed method and all baselines, supporting the claim that cross-stage supervision is broadly useful.

Dataset scale (13,200 designs) is substantially larger than earlier hand-crafted-feature works (<100 designs), improving the credibility of generalization claims relative to prior graph-based baselines.

Reasonably thorough experimental comparison against both graph-based (XGBoost, GNN) and LLM-based (CodeV variants) baselines, with an ablation isolating the contribution of each pretraining task and consistent gains reported across MAE/MAPE/R2/RRSE for both area and delay, with and without KD.
weaknesses: No reported variance across seeds/splits, no significance testing, and only a single 80/20 train/val split is used -- given regression metrics with claimed ~0.1 R2 improvements, it is unclear whether these gains are robust or within noise, especially since neural training on this scale can be sensitive to initialization.

The comparison to VeriDistill is indirect: the paper reimplements CodeV embeddings with its own MLP head rather than reproducing VeriDistill's exact pipeline/dataset/splits, and it is unclear whether the same train/val partition, hyperparameter tuning effort, and preprocessing were applied equally to baselines and StructRTL, raising concerns about a fair and reproducible comparison.

Key hyperparameters (mask ratio 20%, k=16 eigenvectors, α=0.5, τ=0.7, μ=0.5, minimum-per-class m in stratified masking) are fixed without ablation or sensitivity analysis, making it hard to assess robustness of the design choices and reproducibility of the reported gains.
The anonymized code/data repository link in the Appendix is left blank/placeholder, undermining reproducibility claims despite the paper's assertion that code is available.

MasterRTL, a directly relevant prior graph-based PPA estimation baseline discussed at length in Related Work, is excluded from the empirical comparison (justified only by its use of a bit-level, post-some-synthesis representation), leaving a gap versus the closest prior structural-feature approach.

No analysis of inference-time/computational efficiency versus LLM-based baselines, which would strengthen the paper's core motivating claim of enabling 'instant feedback' compared to LLM embedding extraction or full synthesis.

Technology-library generalization is untested: all synthesis/KD experiments use a single PDK (SkyWater 130nm), so it's unclear whether the learned structural representations and distillation benefits transfer to other libraries or technology nodes.

Limited discussion of failure modes, scalability to very large designs (up to 19k nodes CDFGs), or cases where structural pretraining might not help (e.g., very small or highly regular designs), despite dataset statistics suggesting a long tail in design size.

strengths: The paper convincingly motivates CDFG over token-based/AST representations for RTL quality estimation, and the empirical results (Tables 1-2) show a clear and consistent margin over both hand-crafted-feature graph baselines and strong LLM-based baselines (VeriDistill/CodeV variants), especially in delay prediction.

The pretraining objectives are thoughtfully adapted to the computational-graph domain: rather than masking raw node/edge features (which can create semantic ambiguity, e.g., masking an Add could equally be a Sub), masking is applied at the post-GNN embedding level, which is a sensible domain-specific design choice with supporting ablations (Appendix E).

Extensive supplementary experiments substantially strengthen the empirical case: architecture ablations, sensitivity to masking/sampling ratios, per-class masked-node accuracy analysis, generalization across functional clusters and design sizes, evaluation on 51 real industrial design pairs (102 modules), inference-latency/memory scaling curves, and a comparison of LLMs operating directly on CDFGs (further isolating whether gains stem from representation or minor confounds).

Dataset construction (13,200 designs from multiple public Verilog corpora, functional simulation filtering) is considerably larger than prior graph-based RTL quality-estimation work (~100 designs), improving statistical reliability of comparisons.

The knowledge distillation from post-mapping netlists is a reasonable, well-motivated mechanism for bridging the RTL-to-gate-level gap and is shown to consistently improve all methods, not just the proposed one, supporting its general validity.

The limitations section (Appendix O) is candid about scalability to very large designs, weaker performance on sequential circuits, and the open problem of cross-technology-node generalization, and proposes a concrete (if preliminary) mitigation (register-boundary partitioning).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a combination of existing techniques (GraphMAE-style masked modeling, MaskGAE-style edge prediction, GPS-style Laplacian positional encodings, VeriDistill-style cross-stage KD) applied to a new representation (CDFG) rather than a fundamentally new method; the novelty is primarily in domain adaptation/engineering rather than new algorithmic insight.

Memory and runtime scale steeply with design size (52GB peak memory and ~200ms latency at 20K nodes), and the proposed mitigation (register-boundary partitioning) is only a preliminary pilot study on a small set of 51 industrial pairs without validation on very large designs (>100K nodes), leaving scalability to true industrial-scale designs unresolved.

The method is only demonstrated on a single technology library (SkyWater 130nm); cross-technology-node transfer, which the paper itself flags as important for practical EDA adoption, is not empirically evaluated, only discussed qualitatively via limited-data experiments.

Masked node modeling accuracy remains modest for many rare but functionally important operator classes (e.g., ~55-60% for comparison/shift operators even with class-balanced strategies), suggesting the self-supervised signal may be weaker than implied by the strong downstream numbers, and the paper does not analyze how per-class pretraining quality correlates with downstream error for specific operator-heavy designs.

No variance/uncertainty is reported across multiple training seeds or dataset splits for the main results (Tables 1-2), making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported R^2/RRSE improvements, particularly given some deltas versus the strongest CodeV baseline could be modest relative to potential run-to-run variance.

Industrial validation, while a nice addition, is limited to pairwise ranking accuracy on only 51 design pairs; absolute area/delay prediction errors on industrial designs (which are more relevant for early feedback use-cases) are not reported.

Reproducibility of CDFG construction relies on a specific toolchain (Yosys, Stagira Verilog parser) and undocumented implementation choices (e.g., exact node-type taxonomy of 32 classes, handling of parameterized/generate constructs), which may complicate independent replication despite the stated code release.
